title: Lecture 12 – Lens
html:
Source: c12 lens.pptx – 39 slides

Lens #1

Diseases #2

  • cataracts.
  • The most frequently diseases
  • katarraktes (downrushing; waterfall)
  • was thought that a congealed fluid from the brain had flowed in front of the lens.
  • Any lens opacity
  • two forms
  • congenital
  • acquired

Congenital cataracts #3

  • Clinical forms
  • (1) capsular and capsule-lenticular cataracts
  • (2) lenticular cataracts

Congenital cataracts #4

  • Capsular and capsulo-lenticular cataracts.
  • involve only a portion of the capsule along side with superficial layers of the lens contents
  • lens opacities
  • anterior as anterior polar cataract
  • posterior as posterior polar cataract

Capsular and capsulo-lenticular cataracts. #5

Congenital cataracts #6

  • Lenticular cataracts.
  • the contents of the lens but not the lens capsule.
  • variants
  • (1) nuclear only the nucleus is opacified;
  • (2) perinuclear or zonular
  • opacity localized perinuclear,
  • lens periphery and the nucleus of the lens remaining clear;
  • (3) total cataract
  • involves +the capsule, cortex, fibers and the nucleus.

Lenticular cataracts. #7

Congenital cataracts #8

  • Etiology
  • the anterior polar cataract
  • corneal perforation during intrauterine development of the faetus when the lens capsule remains long time in contact with the cornea
  • the posterior polar cataract
  • maintenance of some rest of the vessels that normally have nourished the lens during early stages of development

Congenital cataracts #9

  • Etiology
  • perinuclear or zonular cataract
  • tetany and spasmophyly
  • total cataract
  • rickets
  • infectious diseases and poisonings, during the first 3 months of pregnancy
  • rubella, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, poliomyelitis, mumps, variola, etc.

Congenital cataracts #10

  • Heredity
  • depends upon the etiological factors.
  • environmental factors (diseases,during the first months of pregnancy),
  • not hereditarily transmitted;
  • Rubella 40–60%.
  • Mumps 10–22%.
  • Hepatitis 16%.
  • toxoplasmosis 5%.
  • hereditary factors (chromosomial anomalies)
  • hereditary.

Congenital cataracts #11

  • Congenital cataract
  • leukocoria
  • Esotropia
  • Oculodigital phenomenon
  • cries when the normal eye is covered.
  • difficulty walking or grasping.
  • surgery as early as possible to avoid amblyopia

Treatment #12

  • as soon as possible,
  • just immediately after diagnosing to avoid ambliopya ;
  • surgical
  • extracapsular extraction of the lens
  • discision of the anterior capsule with aspiration of the lens contents or phacoemulsification
  • contact lenses
  • implantation of the intraocular lens
  • after 3-4 years of age,(developing the eye is completed)

Acquired cataracts #13

  • (1) etiology and pathogenesis incomplete elucidated
  • juvenile (<45 years),
  • presenile (45 and 60 years)
  • senile (>60 years)
  • (2) known etiopathogenesis
  • pathological,
  • traumatical
  • secondary cataracts.

Senile cataracts #14

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • above 60 years of age
  • diminishing the visual acuity
  • seeing only shades of gray,
  • blurred vision, distorted vision,
  • glare or star bursts,
  • monocular diplopia,
  • altered color perception,
  • white-greysh color of the pupil

Senile cataracts #15

  • Clinical forms
  • Cortical soft cataract,
  • occurs at first in the lens periphery
  • within 2-3 years the lens opacifies completely.
  • Nuclear hard cataract,
  • beginns within the nucleus
  • has a long evolution of 8-10 years;
  • the lens becomes never totally opacified.
  • Subcapsular cataract
  • anterior
  • posterior more commonly

Senile cataracts #16

  • Cortical cataract
  • the early stage
  • subjectively
  • slow decrease in visual acuity,
  • myodesopsia, monocular diplopia,
  • transient myopia that leads to the reduction of presbyopia.
  • Objectively,
  • fine cuneiform or spiculiform opacities , peripherally in the anterior, posterior or equatorial cortex.
  • grayish-white on the biomicroscopic examination,
  • black on the pink background of the pupil on the
  • biomicroscopic examination,
  • ophthalmoscopic examination;

Senile cataracts #17

  • Cortical cataract
  • the stage of intumescence
  • due to water absorption, the lens becomes intumescent, bulging.
  • Visual acuity is greatly reduced, sometimes until fingers count
  • Objectively,
  • the pupil is grayish white,
  • the lens has an icy appearance.
  • biomicroscopic examination,
  • the opacified lens fibers appear torn by liquid layers,
  • the anterior chamber is shallow due to the bulging of the lens.
  • The iris is pushed forward due to the increase in volume of the lens
  • can lead to acute secondary glaucoma;

Senile cataracts #18

  • Cortical cataract
  • the stage of maturity
  • the opacification of all the lens layers,
  • the excess water is eliminated and the lens returns to its normal volume.
  • Subjectively,
  • visual acuity
  • shadow of the hand ,light sensation
  • Objectively,
  • the anterior chamber is of normal depth,
  • the pupillary field is greyish white
  • the lens is completely opacified with an icy appearance;

Senile cataracts #19

  • Cortical cataract
  • the stage of hypermaturity (Morgagnian cataract)
  • the degeneration and liquefaction of the fibers from the cortex with their fragmentation into protein particles milky white appearance of the lens content.
  • The nucleus falls in the down half of the lens.
  • the capsule, becomes permeable and allows the passage of proteins outside the lens,
  • secondary phacolytic glaucoma, by obstructing the trabeculun
  • Visual acuity shadow of the hand or light sensation.

Nuclear hard cataract, #20

  • opacities in the nucleus, the cortical layers remaining transparent.

Nuclear hard cataract, #21

  • Subjectively,
  • a decrease in visual acuity, especially in intense light.
  • The darkness through the mydriasis improves visual acuity.
  • myopia , due to the condensation of the lens nucleus, which gradually progresses reaching -6-1o diopters.
  • Objectively,
  • no change in pupil color in daylight.
  • biomicroscope,
  • the nucleus appears gray or with a brown-reddish reflex due to the deposition of melanic pigment at the level of the nucleus.
  • ophthalmoscope,
  • a gray pupillary shadow

Subcapsular cataract #22

  • Anterior opacities below the anterior capsule
  • metaplasia of the anterior lens epithelium.
  • Posterior before the posterior capsule
  • migration of the cells of the anterior crystalline epithelium.
  • Functionally,
  • problems adapting to strong sunlight or headlights.
  • a decrease in near visual acuity.

Senile cataracts #23

  • Treatment
  • surgery as soon as visual acuity impairs to carry on with daily activities,
  • intratracapsular extraction of the lens
  • Not done anymore

Senile cataracts #24

  • Treatment
  • extracapsular extraction of the lens (EEC) with implantation of a posterior chamber lens
  • phacoemulsification
  • discision of the anterior capsule with aspiration of the lens contents

Pathological cataracts #25

  • Etiology
  • systemic diseases
  • ocular diseases (complicated cataracts )

Pathological cataracts #26

  • Etiology
  • systemic diseases
  • metabolic disorders
  • diabetes, especially in young people and adults, spontaneous or parathyroid hypocalcemia (posterior subcapsular opacities),
  • endocrine disorders - hypothyroidism, pituitary disorders,
  • dermatological disorders - Rothmund's syndrome, scleroderma, Besnier's diathetic prurigo, chronic eczema,
  • Down's syndrome ,
  • hepato-lenticular Wilson, degeneration
  • general toxics - ergotamine, dinitrophenol, corticosteroids, gold salts
  • local corticoids or miotics
  • common characteristics :
  • always bilateral,
  • located in the same layer of fibers,
  • appear in young people and adults, evolve rapidly towards maturity.

Pathological cataracts #27

  • Etiology
  • ocular diseases (complicated cataracts )
  • iridocyclitis with recurrences, choroiditis,
  • pigmentary retinopathy,
  • retinal detachment, myopia,
  • glaucoma, intraocular tumors
  • common characteristics:
  • always unilateral,
  • start in the superficial cortex,
  • show a characteristic polychromatic glow
  • always evolutionary

Pathological cataracts #28

  • Treatment
  • treatment of associated ocular and systemic diseases
  • surgery
  • EEC with implantation of posterior chamber intraocular lens

Traumatic cataracts #29

  • Etiology
  • blunt trauma (concusion cataract)
  • after several hours or years later.
  • anterior or posterior subcapsular, with a stellate appearance.
  • the capsule is apparently intact;

Traumatic cataracts #30

  • Etiology
  • penetrating lesions of the globe with or without retention of the intraocular foreign body;
  • If the capsule tear is large, the fibers herniate into the anterior chamber.
  • anaphylactic uveitis or a secondary phacogenetic glaucoma;
  • physical agents
  • thunder bolt,
  • radiations (X and beta rays, infrared )
  • Treatment
  • surgical
  • depending upon etiology, clinical forms of the lesions and age of the patient.
  • extracapsular (phacoemulsification) and PC IOL

Secondary cataracts #31

  • posterior lens capsule opacify
  • after extracapsular extraction
  • incomplete resorption of a direct traumatic cataract
  • Treatment
  • surgery (capsulectomy or capsulotomy)
  • YAG laser therapy.

Displacements of the lens #32

  • congenital and acquired.
  • Congenital (ectopies),
  • bilateral and more frequently supero-temporal.
  • Marfan, Marchesani or in homocystinuria.
  • Aquired :
  • (1) partial or subluxated,
  • the lens, although displaced, still remains in the pupillary field;
  • (2) total or lens dislocations,
  • the lens leaves the pupillary field.

Displacements of the lens #33

  • Aquired :
  • etiopathogenesis :
  • a. strong traumas of the eyeball;
  • b. pathological causes:
  • mechanical rupture of Zinn's zonule (tumors, buphthalmia),
  • inflammatory disintegration of Zinn's zone (panophthalmia, chronic choroiditis),
  • degeneration or atrophy of the zonule (strong myopia, retinal detachment, senility, hypermature cataract).

Displacements of the lens #34

  • Subluxation of the lens.
  • Clinically,
  • a decrease in visual acuity,
  • myopia, monocular diplopia.
  • Signs
  • the anterior chamber is uneven in depth,
  • iridodonesis, iridophacodonesis,
  • the possible presence of a vitreous in the anterior chamber,
  • after pupil dilation the equator of the lens can be seen in the pupillary area:

Displacements of the lens #35

  • Subluxation of the lens.
  • evolution can be marked by the secondary glaucoma.
  • treatment
  • surgical
  • indicated in the presence of secondary glaucoma.

Dislocation of the lens. #36

  • the total displacement of the lens from its socket.
  • (1) anterior
  • sudden decrease in visual acuity
  • severe eye pain,
  • corneal irritation through the contact of the lens with the corneal endothelium,
  • acute secondary glaucoma through the mechanical blocking of the cameral angle by dislocated lens.
  • Objectively,
  • deeper anterior chamber ,
  • the lens appears like a drop of oil in water, in the anterior chamber.
  • The treatment is emergency
  • extraction of the lens

Dislocation of the lens. #37

  • (2) posterior – in the vitreous
  • Subjectively,
  • sudden decrease in visual acuity or an improvement in visual acuity if the dislocated lens has been opacified.
  • Objectively,
  • the deep anterior chamber,
  • iridodonesis (trembling movement of the iris in the absence of the lens support),
  • the absence of the lens from its socket .
  • the presence of the dislocated lens in the vitreous
  • complications:
  • phacoanaphylactic uveitis
  • secondary phacogenetic glaucoma.
  • surgical treatment to extract the lens

Dislocation of the lens. #38

  • (3) subconjunctival.
  • after violent contusive traumas that lead to subconjunctival scleral tears near the limbus with expulsion of the subconjunctival lens.
  • Subjectively,
  • intense eye pain and vision loss.
  • Objectively,
  • palpebral edema,
  • subconjunctival blood suffusion,
  • lenticular bulging of the conjunctiva ,
  • the anterior chamber of the eye is full of blood - hemophthalmia
  • Hypotonic eye
  • Emergency surgical intervention
  • removal of the lens and suturing of the scleral wound.
  • the eyeball is functionally compromised.

Correction of aphakia #39
